applied.quote: A Roth accepts only money, not property such as UTMA shares, and its 2025 limit is the smaller of $7,000 or the child's earned income, because UTMA interest and dividends do not count as compensation ([IRS Publication 590-A](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590a)).
applied.replacement: A Roth accepts only money, not property such as UTMA shares, and its 2025 limit is the smaller of $7,000 or the child's earned income; UTMA interest and dividends do not count as compensation ([IRS Publication 590-A](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590a)).
applied.why: SOURCE does not say the limit exists because UTMA income isn't compensation.

applied.quote: Selling UTMA investments to raise that cash can create taxable gains under the [kiddie tax](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc553), though a gift can supply the cash as long as the child has earnings to match.
applied.replacement: Selling UTMA investments to raise that cash can create taxable gains under the [kiddie tax](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc553), and contributions stay capped at the child's earned income.
applied.why: Gift funding the Roth is not in the closed fact list.
